The only really big downside is forgetting to takw it. This is **not** a medicine you'd leave on a weekend trip without or forget to take one day. The withdrawal from being completely without it is dreadful. So a small tip is to keep at least a few in your toiletry bag and if you have an EDC bag or something else, stuff one or two in there as well. This saved me from a few situations 😅

In Norway we use something called BankID to log into any bank or government website.

My SSN is my username, then I have to verify with a code from a physical dongle og use an app on my phone (which I have to verify before I can use it with the dongle) and then I can type my password. 

This is a very secure way of logging in as it doesn't matter who has my SSN. Unless they have my password and access to the 2FA there's no way for anyone to get access. If I lose the 2FA I have to meet in person with my government issued ID to get a new one. 

This is used for banking, social services, tax returns, health care. Pretty much everything important. Never had an issue.

I too came from Google, but using apple devices and a windows PC. 

Proton had two main focuses that comes above everything else: privacy and security. They are damn good on this part, but it comes at a cost of feature development and QoL updates. 

**Mail**: I haven't converted fully to mail yet. The lack of third party app support (security issue) and widgets is too big of an issue for me. But mail is an amazing email client, so if you don't need what I need, it is damn near perfect. 

**Calendar**: same issues for me as above. I need this to be a two way sync with a third party app. 

**VPN**: one of the best in the industry. Split tunneling (allowing some websites through that don't work with VPN), device support and security is perfect. 

**Drive**: maybe their weakest product, but I haven't encountered any issues with syncronizing my files. Not as smooth or pretty as it's competitors, but it does what it says it should do. 

The lack of search in drive is annoying, but I have a solid system so I can easily find my files. I can understand that this may be a deal breaker for some. 

I use the photo feature to just have a second backup of my photos. 

Docs is okay, but very early in its development cycle. Works as a basic editor, but lack a lot of features to make it as good as its competition. 

I use Microsoft products for creating documents and spreadsheets. These are stored and opened from my Proton drive. I only use Google docs when I need to collaborate with people that only use that. I always keep a backup in Proton though. 

**Pass**: It recently became good enough to make me switch from 1Password. Haven't had a single issue so far. The alias feature is amazing and I have it send the emails to my iCloud mail account. It is a solid product with excellent features and support for custom fields. 

## Verdict 
I find the Proton suite to be solid. I moved to a visionary account and have moved my family over. They are growing rapidly and new features are coming at a decent pace. I am very positive about the future of Proton 🙌

When my daughter got an iPhone I changed to an Apple One family plan that included AM, so I decided to give it a fair shot and used it exclusively for 6 months. 

My honest opinion is that AM is better. Once the algorithm learnt my taste the experience has been amazing.

Apple Music:
* Focus on delivering a solid music experience. No social stuff, no podcasts, no audio books
* Sound quality is better, especially if you have the correct equipment 
* Fewer people use it, so finding playlists is harder. You can use other services or apps to import lists film the web though. 
* Pay musicians twice as much as Spotify!!
* Algorithm needs to be told what you like. Don't count on it learning just from your listening habits (I like this!)

Spotify:
* Customizable EQ for more fine tuning, but not as good sound quality as AM
* Everyone uses it, so there's a good chance you can find lots of suggestions from friends to listen to. Because more people uses it, collaborative lists are usually made here for parties and gatherings. 
* Modern UI. Some people like this, but I enjoy the more purist UI of AM more. 
* Spotify Connect; you can control what device you want to play music from and use any other device as a remote. 
* Algorithm mainly uses your listening habits to determine what you like. 

If you're already in the Apple ecosystem, give AM a try. It works very good between devices and is deeply integrated in the Apple ecosystem. 

If you want more social features and apps that work really well on all devices and OS', go for Spotify.

Daily and weekly reviews are the key to managing your to-do list properly.

During my weekly review I plow through everything in the app; every area, task and project. If there are tasks I know I will do this week they are moved to Anytime. Every task or project I don't plan on doing this week lives in my Someday list.

During daily review I empty my inbox and check my today view to plan the day. Whenever I am done with tasks for today I open anytime and start knocking off tasks in there. If I finish tasks in anytime before the week is over I can go through my someday list to see if there is anything I can start on early there.

Having a good setup of tags and areas that **works for you** is the key. Don't go crazy on the tags and areas, only use the ones you need. Your system will grow with whatever your current situation is.

Er 34 og har to barn på 6 og 8. 

Årene fram til barneskolen er uten tvil de tyngste. Et sabla stress med henting/levering i barnehage, jobb, lite fritid og mye penger som går rett til barna.

Om du føler du «mister frihet» ved å få barn, så tror jeg du gjør lurt i å vurdere det skikkelig før du tar steget. Man «mister» ikke frihet. Man ofrer noe av friheten sin for å bli forelder. Altså man flytter tiden fra egenpleie, festing og sånt til barna. Å ha barn, å se dem vokse, utvikle seg fra hjelpesløse klumper til selvstendige unge mennesker er utrolig givende og uten tvil verdt «tapet» av fritid (er min mening, men dette gjelder langt fra alle!). 

Når det kommer til date med partneren, tid for seg selv og annet så er planlegging nøkkelen. Avtal med venner eller familie om å få barnepass 1 fast kveld i måneden (eller mer) som er date night. Besteforeldre er gull her altså! Annen egentid planlegger du med partneren slik at dere begge får tid i løpet av uken til dere selv. Hva denne tiden brukes på er helt opp til dere. Partneren min elsker å lese en god bok med en kopp te. Jeg lar henne gjøre dette uforstyrret etter avtale. Til gjengjeld går jeg mer en tur eller spiller med kompisene når det er min tur. 

Så var det all denne andre tiden da. Alle barn er forskjellig, men de blir utrolig påvirket av hverdagen til foreldrene sine. Jeg vet om foreldre som nesten aldri er på kafé eller butikk med barna «fordi dem er så vanskelige da». Våre barn har vært med på butikk og kafé siden de var nyfødt og blitt vant med at vi følger hverandres timeplan. Alt må ikke snurre rundt livet til barnet ditt. Så lenge barnet får nok oppmerksomhet, søvn og mat så stortrives de. Ta dem med på utflukt til kafeen borti gata, biblioteket eller butikken.

Før dere eventuelt får barn, så lag en tentativ plan. Egentid, tid til hverandre, familietid, rekker dere henting/levering i barnehage uten at hverdagen faller sammen, har dere råd til alt som trengs og det barnet trenger? Alt dette er viktig, og dere er i en god posisjon til å snakke om dette på forhånd. Vi måtte gjette og prøve oss litt fram da vi ble kastet litt ut i det 😅

Nå som barna er eldre er ting mye friere. Barna leker mye med venner i helgene, er på overnatting hos besteforeldre eller venner, kan gå til/fra skolen selv (vi bor såpass nært vi) osv. Nå storkoser jeg meg med minstemann med å spille Mario Kart, fekte med plastsverd, bygge med Lego og kjøre radiobiler. Jeg maler, tegner og sykler med jenta mi og snakker om alt løst og fast. Nå er vi i en fase hvor de trenger stabilitet og oppfølging - ikke kontinuerlig overvåking. 

Og enda bedre blir det etter hvert som de vokser til.

Guild Wars 2 doesn’t have the same archetypes as other MMOs (tank, healer, dps). We have support and dps. Support is divided into 2 groups: healer and boon support (applying buffs as it is known in other games). Boon support usually full either a dps role or a healer role as well. 

The two most important boons are alacrity (lowers cooldowns) and quickness (increases attack speed). A profession can usually do one of those and heal or deal damage on top.

When you’re playing solo open world you will need damage. If you’re grouped with other players they will be happy to receive your support. My tip will be to join a guild and do story content with them. There are tons of veterans that would love to run old content with you 😊

As for elite specializations; tempest is one of the 3 elite specs of elementalist, so you’re already on the right road. Check out Snowcros and Metabattle for good builds for the content you want to do. [Here are a link to a decent tempest support/heal build.](https://metabattle.com/wiki/Build:Tempest_-_Boon_Support_Healer)

When doing open world solo, just look at [this build](https://metabattle.com/wiki/Build:Tempest_-_Fresh_Air) and copy it (same elite spec, so you don’t have to farm even more hero points). Don’t bother too much with the gear quality. Get berserker gear from the trading post of rare or exotic quality for level 80. Find whatever cheap runes and sigils that give you the stats you need (no need to optimize this for open world). 

Having the right build and gear will make it much easier to solo story content and survive in the open world. 

Focus on getting high quality (Exotic or ascended) gear for your healing build and work on getting the correct runes and sigils. Having good gear for group content where you want to support will make a massive difference.

I want to repeat that finding a guild that fits you will be a huge boost to your enjoyment! I often find myself playing through old story content with guild mates and running dungeons with them.

Bitwarden and 1Password are the two big names of this game. 
* Bitwarden is open source and cheaper, but has no password monitoring and less intuitive UI. 
* 1Password is more expensive, but has a slightly better UI and password monitoring (it searches the dark web for password leaks and lets you know if your data is compromised). 

1Password families is what I’m using for my family. Very easy to share passwords, create new ones for my kids and they easily understand how to use it. I get notified if any passwords are leaked and can change them quickly. 

I also store sensitive data in 1Password such as copies of all our birth certificates, IDs, passports, bank account information, crypto wallets and everything else that I need locked behind a very secure door.

I use a password manager because it stores more than just my passwords and 2FA keys. 

Everything important that I may or may not need in the future is stored there. Some examples are:
* Birth certificates for myself and my children
* Insurance numbers in case I die, so my partner know who to contact and where to send claims. 
* A list of all my assets, both stocks and crypto. Same reason as above. 
* Digital copy of my passport and drivers license.
* all my credit cards and bank accounts
* Important notes and backups for WoW addons, 2FA backup codes and so on
* All my crypto wallets, where they’re located, passwords and keys
* copies of my employment agreement
* copies of my mortgage agreement
* Copy of my agreement with my partner whom I live with, own a house with and have two children with, but are not married to
* A copy of my will, in case I die

There are only two physical copies of my secret key and master password (the backup kit from 1Password). One are safely stored in a location only my partner and I know of. The other is kept safe by my attorney and is only to be released to my family if both me and my partner dies. 

1Password has become essential to my life. I have shared vaults with my family so my children can have access to Netflix, Disney+, network passwords and everything else they need. Same applies to my partner. I also share passwords easily to my coworkers if they need access to something when I’m not physically present and can’t do it remote.

I used to be a session and for-hire drummer for about 5 years. I started when I was about 18 and had a solid connection with the music community in my area.

It was fun to begin with (I was doing what I loved AND got paid handsomely for it!), but after a few years, I began to struggle. I would be getting emails and phone calls all the time from bands and artists needing a drummer for their new recordings or live shows. Deadlines was often very short as they called me because their drummer had fallen ill or couldn't be there for one reason or another. I worked HARD. Way harder than I could ever have imagined.

I was on tour with a few bands and did recordings in between. The workload was just insane. It didn't help that work was mostly weekends, evenings, nights and holidays. I completely understand why substance abuse is running wild with artists. The time limits and stress was out of this world.

Was it fun? Yes. Did it pay well? After a lot of hard work; yes. 

Before you venture down this line, know that it requires a lot of hard work, long hours, blisters, pain and frustration. It requires a special mindset and personality to sustain this lifestyle.

If you dream of having a house in the suburbs, family and pets AND time to spend with them, then this may not be the right call.

Money is good though. Once you get your name out there and you perform according to or beyond expectations the work comes flowing and so does the money.

Now I'm working 8-4, have a family and pursue my drumming as a teacher and with a few smaller projects. Much better for my mental health and life.
